questions.question: Explain the difference between for...of and for...in. Which one would you use for an array, and which for an object?
questions.answer:
for...of iterates the values produced by an iterable's iterator: arrays give elements, strings give characters, Map gives [key, value] pairs, Set gives values. It respects break and continue, cannot go out of bounds, and throws TypeError on a plain object because objects are not iterable by default.

for...in iterates the enumerable property keys of an object, as strings, and includes keys inherited through the prototype chain. That makes it suitable for walking an object's keys (with an Object.hasOwn guard or Object.keys instead), but wrong for arrays: you get "0", "1" as strings plus any custom properties, and the order is not the array order you expect. Rule of thumb: for...of for values, Object.keys/entries for object keys, and avoid for...in unless you specifically need inherited enumerable keys.
key_points: for...of reads iterable values and supports break/continue
for...in reads enumerable keys as strings, including inherited ones
Plain objects are not iterable — use Object.keys/entries
Never use for...in on an array

questions.question: When would you choose for, while, do...while, or an array method? Give one concrete situation for each.
questions.answer:
Use for when you know the number of passes or need the index and a custom step, such as iterating a matrix by row and column. Use while when the number of iterations is unknown and the condition should be tested before the body, such as retrying a request until it succeeds or reading until a buffer is empty. Use do...while when the body must run at least once, such as displaying a menu before asking whether to continue. Use map/filter/reduce when you are transforming an array into a new value and do not need early exit, because they express intent and avoid manual index bookkeeping. Use for...of as the default for arrays when you only need values.

The decision is about the shape of the problem: known count → for, unknown count → while, at-least-once → do...while, transform → array method. If you need to stop early, for...of with break or .find() is clearer than forEach, which cannot break.
key_points: for: known count, index, custom step
while: unknown count, test before the body
do...while: body must run at least once
Array methods for transforms; for...of for early exit

questions.answer:
It prints [ 3, 3, 3 ], then [ 0, 1, 2 ].

var is function-scoped (or global here), so there is one i shared by all three closures. By the time the callbacks run, the loop has finished and i is 3. let is block-scoped and the for header creates a fresh binding for each iteration, so each closure captures its own j — 0, 1, and 2.

This is the classic "loop closure bug". Before let, the fix was an IIFE or a local const copy inside the loop. If you need the value at push time, you can also write for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) { const current = j; b.push(() => current); }.
key_points: var: one shared function-scoped binding
let in a for header: fresh binding per iteration
All var callbacks see the final value, 3
Fix with let, an IIFE, or a local const copy

questions.answer:
It prints:
number one
string one
string one
other

switch compares with strict equality, so the number 1 matches case 1 but never the string "1". When describe(1) matches case 1 there is no break, so execution falls through and also runs case "1" before hitting its break — hence two lines for the numeric call.

describe("1") matches the string case directly and prints one line. describe(2) matches nothing and runs default. To avoid the fallthrough, put a break or return after every case, or group empty cases deliberately. Also remember switch does not coerce, so "1" and 1 are different cases.
key_points: switch uses strict equality, no coercion
Missing break falls through to the next case
describe(1) prints both number and string messages
Add break/return or group empty cases intentionally

questions.answer:
It logs 0 Kakade, 1 Asha, extra x, then own and inherited.

for...in walks enumerable property keys, not array values. On an array it gives the indexes as strings, and because arrays are objects, any custom property such as arr.extra is included too. On an object it also walks the prototype chain, so the inherited key appears.

The fix for arrays is for...of, which reads values and ignores extra properties: for (const name of arr) console.log(name). If you need indexes, use arr.entries() or a classic for loop. For objects, use Object.keys(child) or Object.entries(child) to get own enumerable keys only, or add if (Object.hasOwn(child, key)) inside a for...in loop when inherited keys are genuinely needed.
key_points: for...in reads keys, not values
Array indexes arrive as strings; custom properties appear
for...in includes inherited enumerable keys
Use for...of for arrays and Object.keys/entries for objects
